title: Orthogonal Ensembles and Tested Explanations for Performer-Independent Body-Motion Emotion Recognition

blocks.text: Naoto Nishida and Yoshio Ishiguro, The University of Tokyo
ACII 2026, MMAC Challenge (Cross-Cultural Emotion Recognition from Body Movements, DIEM-A), oral

notes: Good morning. I'm Naoto Nishida from the University of Tokyo, and this is joint work with Yoshio Ishiguro. The paper is about reading emotion from body motion alone, and it has two halves that carry equal weight. The first is an ensemble that works because its members disagree with each other. The second is a set of explanations that we test instead of only drawing. At the end I'll show that both halves come from the same structure in the data. About twelve minutes, then I'm happy to take questions.

title: Reading emotion from body motion alone
leadIn: Twelve acted emotions from skeleton motion, with no face, no audio and no scene, scored on performers the model never trained on.

blocks.text: Two takeaways: an ensemble gains when its members' errors disagree, and explanations can be tested.

notes: The task is to name one of twelve acted emotions from skeleton motion. No face, no audio, no scene, just how the body moves. The part that makes it hard is the split: every test clip comes from a person the model never saw in training. Chance is 8.3 percent, and a strong skeleton baseline only reaches about 25. So there is plenty of headroom, but the problem is genuinely underdetermined. If you take two things away from the talk, take these: ensembles win when the members' errors disagree, and explanations can be tested rather than only visualized.

title: The setting is the hard part, not the model
leadIn: Across performers, the same emotion varies about as much as different emotions vary within one performer.

items: Semantically close emotions share kinematics: jealousy with contempt, shame with guilt.
A reproduced STGCN++ baseline reaches 25.73 ± 4.03% Macro-F1 on this split, against 8.3% chance.

blocks.text: Leave-performers-out: every test clip comes from a person the model never saw in training.

notes: Why is it so hard? Two reasons. First, emotions that are close in meaning are close in movement. Jealousy and contempt look alike; shame and guilt look alike. Second, everyone has a personal movement style, so the same emotion performed by two people can vary about as much as two different emotions performed by one person. Under leave-performers-out, our reproduced STGCN++ baseline reaches 25.73 percent Macro-F1, plus or minus about four. That is the number every later comparison is measured against, because we reproduced it on exactly the same 74-performer split. A single better architecture does not have much room to move here.

title: What did not work
leadIn: Under leave-performers-out, every obvious single-model upgrade failed or went backwards.

items: A supervised-contrastive head cost −11.53 pp.
Scenario-text alignment lost 1.42 pp and its projection collapsed onto performer identity.
A vision-language model ranked the true class last on faceless, scene-free skeletons.
Post-hoc calibration moved the score by 0 to −0.14 pp.

items.label: best single model
items.note: the ceiling of the single-model route

blocks.text: These negatives are why we went for diversity instead of one better model. The paper catalogues eight of them.

notes: We did try the obvious single-model upgrades. A supervised-contrastive head, which cost eleven and a half points, because twelve classes in a batch of 128 leave too few positives per class. Scenario-text alignment, whose projection collapsed onto performer identity instead of emotion. Distillation from a vision-language model, which ranked the true class last on faceless skeleton renderings. Post-hoc calibration, which moved nothing. The best single model we could build tops out at about 30 percent. We report these on purpose. They are not an embarrassment, they are the reason we stopped trying to find one better architecture and went for diversity instead.

title: Combine models that make different mistakes
leadIn: Four model families with different built-in assumptions, averaged as raw scores.

blocks.text: Graph networks, an attention model, hybrid MLPs and frozen external pretraining fail on different clips. We average their logits with equal weight.

notes: So the design is simple. Take four families that carry different assumptions about motion, graph networks, an attention model, hybrid MLPs, and some frozen external pretraining, and average their raw pre-softmax scores. Equal weight, nothing fitted, nothing to tune. Eleven members, about thirteen million trainable parameters in total, and inference is eleven forward passes over a 64-frame clip followed by a mean. The bet is that the gain comes from the members disagreeing, not from the extra parameters. The next three slides are me trying to show that the bet is right.

title: +11.07 pp over a baseline we reproduced on the same split
leadIn: The eleven-model ensemble reaches 36.80 ± 4.00% Macro-F1 where the same-split baseline reaches 25.73 ± 4.03%.

blocks.text: The paired-fold improvement excludes zero in 10 of 10 folds, and resampling whole performers keeps it above zero.
This is 10-fold cross-validation on the labeled training performers. The hidden-test result is still pending.

95% CI on the gain: [9.86, 12.33] pp by fold, [9.14, 12.17] pp by performer. The official 92-performer baseline, 25.21 ± 4.49%, sits within one SD of our reproduction and serves only as an external anchor.

notes: Here is the headline. The eleven-model ensemble reaches 36.80 percent Macro-F1, against 25.73 for the baseline on the same split. That is eleven points and change, about 43 percent relative. It is not noise: the paired improvement excludes zero in all ten folds, and it survives resampling whole performers rather than folds. Two honest framings. This is cross-validation on the training performers, and the hidden-test leaderboard number is still pending, so this is a development finding and not a benchmark placement. And the official baseline is an external anchor only. Our reproduction sits within one standard deviation of it, which is why the comparison is same-split.

title: The gain builds one family at a time
leadIn: Baseline, best single model, seven-way, eleven-way: 25.7 → 30.1 → 33.9 → 36.8%.

blocks.text: Ensembling beats the best single model by +6.8 pp. Averaging logits instead of probabilities adds a further +1.15 pp at no cost.
The +1.15 pp is not a scaling artifact: z-scored fusion keeps +0.99 pp and rank-only Borda keeps +0.69 pp. Bars carry ±SD and bootstrap 95% CIs over 10 folds, with per-fold points behind them.

notes: Now the why. This chart walks the gain up in stages: the reproduced baseline, the best single model, a seven-way ensemble, and the eleven-way system we submitted. Each family adds a step. Ensembling beats the best single model by almost seven points, which is already more than any architecture change bought us. And averaging the logits rather than the probabilities is worth a further point and a bit, for free. That is not a scaling trick: if we z-score the members first we keep most of it, and if we throw away the magnitudes entirely and fuse ranks we still keep about two thirds.

title: The members rarely fail on the same clip
leadIn: Averaging cancels a mistake only when the members do not repeat it together, and the lift is spread across branches.

items: Pairwise error correlations run from 0.15 to 0.43, lowest for the frozen external branches.
Removing any single member costs between −0.84 and −0.09 pp.
Removing all four external members at once costs −2.91 pp.

blocks.text: Correlations are Pearson correlations of per-sample error indicators over 7,992 out-of-fold clips. Leave-one-out deltas are on pooled out-of-fold Macro-F1, base 36.94%.

notes: This is the mechanism. On the left, every pair of members, coloured by how often they are wrong on the same clip. Everything sits between 0.15 and 0.43, which is low, and the lowest column is the frozen external pretraining, the branch that is least like the others. On the right, what happens when you take one member out: every single bar is negative, from about four fifths of a point down to a tenth. Nobody dominates and nobody is dead weight. Take the whole external block out at once and you lose almost three points. One caution: moderate correlation is not redundancy. The two correlated MAMP models still give the largest single contribution.

title: The mistakes land between confusable emotions
leadIn: Residual errors fall between confusable emotions, jealousy into contempt and guilt into sadness, matching a top confidence near 62%.

items: The Japan and Taiwan difference (35.3 vs 38.9%) is a dataset stratum, tangled with capture era and personal style.
Dropping the seven earliest Japanese training performers moves the score by −0.44 pp.

blocks.text: The country difference is not a cultural finding.
Era check: 36.50 vs 36.94% pooled out-of-fold. Performer country is decodable from contact-marker features at 69.8%, which is one reason the country split cannot carry a cultural reading.

notes: A quick sanity check on what the system still gets wrong. The residual errors sit between emotions that are genuinely confusable: jealousy goes to contempt, guilt goes to sadness or shame. That matches the model's top confidence, which stays around 62 percent. One thing I want to be careful about. The dataset has Japanese and Taiwanese performers, and their scores differ. That is a dataset stratum, tangled with capture era and individual movement style, and we do not read it as culture. As an era check we drop the seven earliest Japanese training performers, and the score moves by less than half a point.

title: Explanations you can test
leadIn: A heatmap asserts. A test can come back negative.

blocks.text: The second half of the talk asks what the model reads, and checks each answer against the prediction.

notes: That is the first half: where the number comes from, and why. The second half is the one I care more about. Most explainability in this area draws a heatmap and asserts that it means something. The trouble is that a decorative attribution looks exactly like a real one, so the picture cannot be wrong. We wanted claims that could come back negative, so we built the explanations as a set of checks with values and nulls attached. Same system, no retraining, and one of the checks does come back negative.

title: Six checks, five positive and one negative
leadIn: For every claim that the model uses a body region, we mask it, perturb it, or edit its motion, and check whether the prediction moves.

blocks.text: Post hoc, no retraining, and no accuracy cost.
Every check runs on a strong ensemble member and is re-run on the submitted 11-way ensemble.

notes: Here is the scorecard. Whenever we want to say the model uses some body region, we do something to that region: mask it, add noise to it, or physically edit its motion, and then we look at whether the prediction actually moves. That gives six checks, each with a value and a null or a confidence interval. Five come back positive. One comes back negative, and we report it, because a test that can only say yes is not a test. All of this is post hoc, so it costs no accuracy, and each check is run on a strong member and then re-run on the full ensemble we submitted.

title: The cited regions actually matter
leadIn: Masking the parts the model calls important hurts more than masking the parts it calls unimportant, and the ranking survives noise at σ = 0.02.

blocks.text: Without these two, the alignment on the next slide would be self-consistent decoration.

notes: The first two checks are the foundation for everything after them. Faithfulness: we rank the body parts by saliency, mask them in that order, and compare against masking in the reverse order. The gap is positive, about 0.124, and positive in every one of the ten folds. At the finer 25-joint resolution it grows to 0.199. Stability: add input noise and the ranking barely moves, with a rank correlation of 0.98, and the top-ranked part never flips. These two matter because without them, the Laban alignment I am about to show would just be a decorative attribution agreeing with itself.

title: The model reads the body the way a movement analyst names it
leadIn: Laban Movement Analysis is how a movement analyst describes motion.

items: Alignment is ρ = +0.500 against +0.033 for classical kinematics, about 15 times stronger.
The bootstrap CI over emotion blocks is [+0.150, +0.733] with permutation p<0.001, and 10 of 12 emotions are positive.
Sadness reads as a bowed, sunken posture: head down, trunk leaning forward.

blocks.text: The emotions are not independent, so the CI bootstraps over emotion blocks and the permutation shuffles region scores within each emotion. Sign test over emotions p = 0.039, median per-emotion ρ = +0.70.

notes: This is the load-bearing result. We take the model's salient regions and ask whether they line up with Laban Movement Analysis, which is the vocabulary a movement analyst uses to describe how a body moves. They do, about fifteen times more strongly than with classical kinematics: 0.500 against 0.033. We are careful with the statistics, because the twelve emotions are not twelve independent observations. The confidence interval bootstraps over emotion blocks and the permutation shuffles within emotions, and the alignment is positive for ten of the twelve. The best part is that it reads in plain language. For sadness, the model looks exactly where you would expect: bowed head, lowered height, trunk leaning forward.

title: It holds for the system we submitted, and edits move the prediction
leadIn: Re-running the same test on the eleven-way ensemble gives an alignment at least as strong as the single member's.

items.label: predictions flipped by freezing the head
audited cards with an unsupported claim

blocks.text: These edits corroborate. They are not causal proof, and the load-bearing number stays the +0.500 against +0.033 alignment.

notes: Two more checks. First, this is not a claim about one lucky model. We re-run the whole thing on the eleven-way ensemble we actually submitted, and the alignment is 0.517, if anything a little stronger, with the interval clear of zero. Second, on the right, we edit the motion itself. Freeze the head and 41 percent of predictions flip. Amplify an arm and 23 percent flip, and the ranking of parts matches what masking told us. I want to be precise about what that buys: this is observational corroboration, not causal proof. The number carrying the argument is still the 0.500 against 0.033 alignment.

title: The negative we report
leadIn: Within a window, no single frame stands out.

items: The important-versus-reverse gap is about +0.002 in time, against +0.124 in space.
Spatial saliency is head-dominant for all twelve emotions, so the evidence is spatial.

blocks.text: This is about locating a frame. Order still matters, and time reversal does move accuracy.
Frame saliency entropy is about 98.7% of log T per sample and 99.5% as a class mean, both close to uniform.

notes: And here is the negative, which I think is what makes the rest of it a test. When we ask which frames inside the window carry the evidence, the answer is all of them, roughly equally. The saliency entropy sits at about 98.7 percent of the maximum, and the important-versus-reverse gap in time is essentially zero, where the same measurement in space gave a clear positive. Across all twelve emotions the spatial picture is head-dominant, so the model's evidence is spatial rather than one decisive moment. To be precise, this is about locating a frame, not about time in general. Order still matters, and time reversal does move accuracy.

title: One idea behind both halves
leadIn: Performance varies about fourfold across people, half intrinsic difficulty and half model-specific error. The ensemble cancels that second half, and the explanations read it.

items: Absolute Macro-F1 is low, so the claim is a matched-protocol +43% relative gain.
The headline is cross-validation on training performers, with the hidden test pending.
Laban alignment is semantic; masking and motion edits test dependence separately.

notes: Let me tie the two halves together. Performance across individual performers varies by roughly a factor of four, and that variation decomposes into about half intrinsic difficulty, the people who are hard for everything, and about half model-specific error, the people one architecture happens to fail on. That second half is precisely what averaging orthogonal members cancels, and it is the same structure the explanations are reading. So one mechanism, showing up twice. Where we are honest: the absolute score is low, so the contribution is relative; the headline is cross-validation with the test pending; and the Laban result is semantic alignment, with dependence tested separately.

title: Orthogonal errors win, and explanations can be tested
leadIn: Thank you. I am happy to take questions.

items: On underdetermined body-motion tasks, the thing to buy is orthogonal errors.
Test your explanations, and report the checks that come back negative.
This model reads body-region motion in Laban terms, and sadness is a bowed, sunken posture.

blocks.text: Naoto Nishida and Yoshio Ishiguro, The University of Tokyo

notes: That is the talk. Two things to carry out of the room. On a task like this one, where the setting is underdetermined and no architecture transfers across strangers, the thing worth buying is orthogonal errors rather than more capacity. And explanations are worth testing, including reporting the test that comes back negative, because that is what makes the positive ones mean something. When we did test them, this model turned out to read body-region motion the way a movement analyst would name it. Thank you, and I am happy to take questions.
